question:
Patient note:
A 28-year-old woman arrived to the ambulatory surgical center this morning for pre-procedure evaluation prior to a planned hysteroscopic resection of a 1.5 cm endometrial polyp discovered during infertility work-up; the gynecology team anticipates a brief operative time under monitored anesthesia care with same-day discharge, and the procedure is regarded as a minor, low-risk operation. She reports feeling well and maintains her usual weekday routine, which includes walking her dog two miles each morning and taking the stairs to her third-floor apartment without limitation. She has not been hospitalized or operated on in the past year and has had no casts, fractures, or traumatic injuries; the only surgeries in her history are a tonsillectomy at age five and wisdom-tooth extraction during college, both uncomplicated. She has had no episodes of sepsis, pneumonia, congestive heart failure, stroke, multiple trauma, or acute spinal cord injury within the past month, and she has not undergone any major surgical procedure during that time frame. Review of systems today is largely unremarkable. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest pain, palpitations, lower-leg edema, chronic cough, recent fever, productive sputum, or shortness of breath. Bowel habits are stable; she was diagnosed with mildly active ileocolic Crohn’s disease six years ago after colonoscopy and biopsy, managed with mesalamine 2.4 g daily and one flare requiring outpatient prednisone taper two years ago. She has been symptom-free since and follows routinely with gastroenterology. No history exists of myocardial infarction, chronic lung disease, malignancy, or connective-tissue disorders. She has never experienced calf tenderness, limb swelling, or pleuritic chest discomfort suggestive of clot, and duplex ultrasound has never been obtained. Extensive laboratory testing performed by her reproductive endocrinologist nine months ago—prompted by two first-trimester miscarriages—identified heterozygosity for the G20210A variant of the prothrombin gene; antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, and homocysteine were within reference ranges, and platelet counts have always been normal. She has not required anticoagulation, and none of her relatives have had unexplained thrombosis or pulmonary embolus. She takes a prenatal multivitamin, mesalamine as noted, and a combined oral contraceptive that will be discontinued after today’s procedure; she uses no selective estrogen modulators or hormone replacement. There have been no central venous ports, tunneled catheters, or peripherally inserted central lines placed at any time. She does not smoke, drinks wine on weekends, and has never used illicit drugs. Vital signs in the pre-operative bay: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. She appears comfortable, converses easily, and ambulation in the hallway is brisk and steady. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung fields are clear to auscultation throughout, and there are no crackles or wheezes. The abdomen is soft, non-distended, and mildly tender to palpation in the suprapubic region corresponding to the known polyp but without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds are active. No hepatosplenomegaly is appreciated. Extremities are warm and well perfused with easily palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally; there is no pitting edema, erythema, varicosities, or calf asymmetry. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact strength and sensation in all four limbs; gait is normal. Skin shows no ulcers or rashes. Recent laboratory values drawn last week include hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, platelet count 245 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 5.8 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 21 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 18 U/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, and potassium 4.1 mmol/L; prothrombin time was 12.6 s with an INR of 1.0 and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. Pregnancy test this morning is negative. Electrocardiogram displays normal sinus rhythm without ST-segment changes. Chest radiography obtained last year for pre-employment screening was clear, and no interval pulmonary issues have developed. Airway assessment is Mallampati class I, thyromental distance adequate, and neck range of motion full; anesthesia does not anticipate airway difficulty. She has been fasting since midnight, has voided without issue, and peripheral IV access was established with a 20-gauge cannula on the first attempt. Sequential compression devices are ready to be applied in the operating room; no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has been initiated prior to incision.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds the points for each qualifying perioperative risk factor:
- Planned minor surgery: brief hysteroscopic polypectomy (+1).
- Current estrogen-containing oral contraceptive: still taking it before surgery (+1).
- Known inherited thrombophilia: heterozygous prothrombin G20210A mutation (+3), even without prior thrombosis.
- History of inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn disease (+1), even when asymptomatic.
Age 28, normal mobility, and two first-trimester miscarriages add no points; the recurrent spontaneous abortion criterion requires at least three. The standard sum is 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 6. Omitting the Crohn disease point gives a subtotal of 5.
Final answer: 5
